Annual Meetings

Morning Session - 2012 Meeting

Warren Buffett assures shareholders that his upcoming treatment for prostate cancer is a "nonevent" and tries to clear up what he sees as misunderstandings over a tax-the-rich proposal that has come to be known as the "Buffett Rule." He also argues that political views shouldn't affect investing decisions and explains why there might be some life left n the newspaper business afterall.

Sat, May 5 2012 • 9:00 AM EDT
Key Chapters —
  1. 10. We'll buy "significantly" undervalued Berkshire shares
  2. 14. Business schools are improving but still teach "nonsense"
  3. 15. Buffett Rule: minimum tax for "very, very high earners"
  4. 18. Political views shouldn't affect investing decisions
  5. 21. Buffett: prostate cancer treatment is "nonevent"
  6. 24. Take advantage when "Mr. Market" acts like a "psychotic drunk"
  7. 33. Buffett sees value in local newspapers
  8. 34. Buffett: Amazon won't affect Nebraska Furniture Mart

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. The â I do believe that the CEO of any large, particularly financial-related, company should â it really should apply beyond that, but certainly with a financially-related company â should be the chief risk officer.

Sync Video to Paragraph

It's not something to be delegated. In fact, Charlie and I have seen that function delegated at very major institutions, and the risk committee would come in and report every week, every month, and they'd report to the directors, and they'd have a lot of nice figures lined up, and be able to talk in terms of how many sigmas were involved and everything, and the place was just ripe for real trouble.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

It's a very important ability. It ranks right up there with allocation of capital and selection of managers for the operating units.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

Now, we have people in charge of our insurance businesses that themselves worry very much about the risk of their own unit and, therefore, the person at the top really has to understand whether those three or four people running the big insurance units are correctly assessing their risks, and then also has to be able to aggregate and think how they accumulate over the units.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, not only was it â this risk decision frequently delegated in America, but it was delegated to people who were using a very silly way of judging risk that they've been taught in some our leading business schools. (Laughter)

So this is a very serious problem this man is raising. The so-called "Value at Risk" and the theories that outcomes in financial markets followed a Gaussian curve, invariably. It was one of the dumbest ideas ever put forward. (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph
